newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dollar recovers from early dip to end steady.
newsitem.headline: NZ dollar recovers from early dip to end steady.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar recovered from a sharp, politically inspired, sell-down on Tuesday with its uptrend largely unscathed.

The currency ended at US$0.7075/82 from its 0.7089/96 open, having been sold down to a low of US$0.7053 after New Zealand First Party Winston Peters leader threw doubts on the future of New Zealand's inflation-controlling framework.

Peters said there was a certain inevitability about the widening of the Reserve Bank's zero to two percent annual inflation band, adding the Labour Party's minus 1.0 to 3.0 percent band would also fail.
NZ First's policy is to maintain inflation at a lower level than New Zealand's trading partners'.
Peters holds the balance of power as the major parties continue coalition talks after the inconclusive October 12 general election.
One dealer said the currency's resilience to what normally would have been heavily bearish news was symptomatic of the sheer weight of buying pressure.
When Kiwi dropped about 20 basis points on Peter's comments, there was no shortage of buyers, they said.
"Basically it is just another political statement which does not see the Kiwi stay down for very long," said one Wellington dealer.
"The interest rates are so high that people just cannot run short positions because it costs too much to fund it," he said.
New Zealand has the highest real interest rates of any comparable western country.
"As long as the fundamentals are reasonably okay, you are not going to get a selloff in this currency unless you get substantially lower interest rates," he said.
"It still looks like that, overall, we are going lower eventually, it's just a matter of figuring out when," he said.
A lower Kiwi may result if and when the Reserve Bank eases monetary policy or serious profit-taking emerges.
The three-year uptrend support line is between 0.6880-0.6900. "Until Kiwi can break below those levels, we are still in that uptrend we've been in since 1993," he said.
